opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated things in building with LLMs. Accuracy, or any single aggregate metric, compresses a lot of behavior into one number. It tells you *how much* the system is failing, but not *why* or *how*, and the why is what you need to actually improve anything.

When you read the outputs, you start seeing patterns a metric would never surface. Maybe the model is getting the right answer for the wrong reason, which means it'll break the moment the distribution shifts a little. Maybe your "errors" are really problems with your labels or your eval set, and the model was arguably correct. Or there's a whole cluster of failures from one cause, like the retrieval step pulling the wrong document, or the model misreading an instruction because of how the prompt was phrased. Each of those needs a completely different fix, and a single accuracy number lumps them all together.

There's also the issue that with generative models, the output space is so open that your metric is often a proxy at best. You might use an LLM judge or some heuristic, and unless you look at the actual outputs, you don't know whether that judge agrees with what you'd consider good. I've seen cases where the number goes up and the system gets worse in ways users would immediately notice, like it gets more verbose, more hedgy, or starts gaming whatever the evaluator rewards.

So my workflow is: look at a bunch of examples early and often, categorize the failures, count them, and then go after the biggest buckets. It sounds tedious, and people want to skip it and jump to trying a bigger model or a fancier technique. But in my experience, an hour of reading outputs saves you days of blindly tweaking things. It also builds intuition. You develop a feel for how the model behaves, and that intuition is what lets you design better prompts, better pipelines, and better evals in the first place.

The metric tells you where you are. The error analysis tells you where to go next.

r003.rationale: It mentions possible label or evaluation-set problems, but does not describe enabling human inspection of data as part of data curation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think accuracy as a number tells you where you are, but it tells you almost nothing about why you're there or what to do next. And that's really the whole game, right? If you're at 70 percent on some benchmark, the number itself doesn't tell you whether the 30 percent you're missing is because the model is making one systematic mistake, or ten different kinds of mistakes, or whether your eval data is actually just wrong.

And honestly, that last one happens way more than people expect. I can't tell you how many times we've looked at the failures and realized a big chunk of them are label noise, or the prompt is ambiguous, or the grader is penalizing something that's actually correct. So you go in thinking you have a model problem and you come out realizing you have a data problem or a measurement problem. You only find that by actually reading the outputs.

The other thing is that when you do read them, you start seeing clusters. You'll notice, oh, the model always fails when the input has this particular structure, or it always gets confused when there are two entities with similar names, or it's hallucinating a tool call that doesn't exist. Those clusters are actionable. You can go write more data for that case, or change how you're constructing the prompt, or add a check. A single aggregate number is never actionable in that way.

I'd also say it builds intuition over time. If you're the person who's read a few thousand model outputs, you develop a feel for what the model is good at and bad at that you just can't get from a dashboard. And that intuition is what lets you make good decisions about what to build next, what to prioritize, what's actually going to move the needle versus what just looks nice in a slide.

So I kind of think of it as, the metric is the compass, but the error analysis is the map. You need both, but if I had to give one up, I'd honestly rather keep reading the outputs.

astra-6.text:
Accuracy tells you how often a model gets something right, but it doesn’t really tell you what it has learned or why it’s getting things wrong. You can have two models with very similar accuracy that make very different kinds of mistakes.

When you actually read the outputs and look at the failures, you start seeing patterns. Maybe the model struggles with a particular type of input. Maybe the labels are ambiguous, or there’s something wrong with the data. Those observations give you a much more concrete idea of what to do next than just watching a metric go up or down.

And I think it builds intuition. You form a hypothesis about what’s going on, look at examples, and see whether that hypothesis holds. Then you can turn what you learn into a better evaluation or a targeted improvement. So I see error analysis and metrics as complementary—you need the number, but you also need to understand what’s behind it.

sol-6.1.text:
Accuracy gives you a useful summary, but it doesn’t tell you what the model is getting wrong or why. You have to look at the outputs and ask: Does this make sense? Are there patterns in the mistakes? Is the problem with the data, the labels, or something the model hasn’t learned?

You might have two models with similar accuracy that behave very differently on the examples you care about. Reading those examples helps you understand that difference and decide what to work on next. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of time improving a number without really understanding whether you’re making the system more useful.
